title: The Delusion of Possession
opening: Maybe nothing here was ever really ours to keep. Maybe it was entrusted to us to love.
prayer: Lord, thank You for everything You have entrusted to me. Forgive me when I confuse Your gifts with possessions I must hold onto forever. Teach me instead to cherish what is in my care today. Let me love the people, abilities, work, moments and years You give me with everything I have, knowing even my ability to love comes from You. As the seasons of my life pass, help me see not only what is leaving, but all that I have been given the privilege to love. And when my own life breath returns to You, may I rest knowing that by Your grace I tried to love well what You placed into my hands. May the life You entrusted to me become my gift of love returned to You, the Giver. Amen.
body:
There is a sadness in today's reading from Ecclesiastes. I don't know how there couldn't be. “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,” it says, and then comes this extraordinary description of aging: the strong men bend, the grinders become few, those looking through the windows grow dim, the almond tree blooms white, the silver cord is snapped, the golden bowl is broken, and finally “the dust returns to the earth as it once was, and the life breath returns to God who gave it.”
At first I read it almost as a description of loss. We live, and while we are living, we are also slowly withering. That is true. Youth passes. Our bodies change. People leave. Careers end. Children grow. Seasons that once seemed permanent suddenly exist behind us. Eventually our own lives come to an end.
There is something deeply sad about that.
But I kept wondering why. If I believe in God, if I believe in resurrection, why does the passing of things still leave such an emptiness? Why do we place so much value on things we know cannot remain? Why do we become so attached to what we have? And why can't knowing what awaits us simply change that feeling?
That question brought me to the word possession.
We get tangled up in what we possess. My home. My work. My body. My time. My family. My life. There is something about “mine” that makes us want to hold tighter because possession carries with it the fear of losing.
But maybe possession is the wrong word.
Entrusted.
That word changed something for me.
What if the things and people that come into our lives are not ours in the sense that we must somehow keep them forever? What if they are entrusted to us? Given into our care so that while they are here, we have the opportunity to love them.
Then the fact that something passes doesn't decrease its value. Maybe the question isn't how do I stop loving something because someday it will leave? Maybe the question is how much can I love what God has entrusted to me while it is here?
That changes the almond tree for me.
Yes, perhaps one day we become the almond tree with its white blossoms, our hair announcing another season of life. Or perhaps our lives end before we ever reach that season. None of us knows. But maybe those white blossoms do not have to represent only what has withered. They can also represent all the seasons that came before them. All that was entrusted. All that was loved.
Maybe our lives are not simply a process of receiving things and then losing them. Maybe they are a process of receiving and loving.
God gives us people to love. He gives us abilities to use. He gives us work, relationships, moments, bodies, places, days and years. We don't control how long any of them remain. But while they are entrusted to us, we can love them.
And somehow that makes me see returning them differently.
What if everything God entrusts to us can eventually be returned to Him carrying the love we gave it?
Not because our love makes something worthy of God, and certainly not because we earn our way back to Him. Even our ability to love comes through His grace. But perhaps He gives us this extraordinary opportunity during our lives to show Him what our loving looks like.
He gives.
We receive.
We love.
And we return.
Maybe that is part of what a life is.
The career I was given the opportunity to have, the people I have cared for, my husband, my children, my home, my body, the people who have crossed my path, even the ordinary days I barely noticed at the time—all entrusted.
And perhaps my responsibility was never to keep any of them from changing. It was to love them while they were within my care.
Then one day I too will be returned.
“The dust returns to the earth as it once was, and the life breath returns to God who gave it.”
That line doesn't feel quite as bleak to me anymore.
The life breath returns to the Giver.
And perhaps when my own time comes, whether I ever become that almond tree covered in white blossoms or whether God calls me before then, what will matter is not how tightly I managed to hold everything together. It will be how much I loved what He entrusted to me.
There is still sadness in Ecclesiastes. I don't think I want to remove it anymore. The sadness exists because these gifts matter. We cherish them because we have known them, touched them, lived among them and loved them.
But maybe growing older doesn't have to be seen only as losing pieces of ourselves along the way. Maybe we can also look back and see what those years held: what we were entrusted with, whom we loved, how we served, where we failed and learned to love better, and how God's grace taught us to love at all.
And perhaps at the end there can be rest in that.
Not because we possessed everything we wanted or managed to keep everything we loved, but because by His grace we were given the chance to love.
Maybe that is the gift God gives us in this short life. He entrusts something of His creation into our hands and lets us show Him what our loving looks like.
And when our hands finally open, what we have loved returns to the Giver.
Not merely as something lost, but as something loved.
